teacher.title: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar
teacher.description: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar (1775–1835), one of the Carnatic trinity, composer of ~500 kṛtis in Sanskrit, known for his mastery of rāga, the navagraha kṛtis, the kamalamba navavarṇa kṛtis, and his use of Sanskrit sahitya with intricate rāga structures; his influence on Carnatic music theory is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar (1775–1835), one of the Carnatic trinity, composer of ~500 kṛtis in Sanskrit, known for his mastery of rāga, the navagraha kṛtis, the kamalamba navavarṇa kṛtis, and his use of Sanskrit sahitya with intricate rāga structures; his influence on Carnatic music theory is represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita
teacher.description: Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita (1613–1697), the Advaita Vedānta scholar and poet, grandson of Appayya Dīkṣita; author of the Śiva-leśa, Śivalīlārṇava, and the satirical Kaliviḍambana; his role in the Śrīvidyā and Advaita traditions in South India is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita (1613–1697), the Advaita Vedānta scholar and poet, grandson of Appayya Dīkṣita; author of the Śiva-leśa, Śivalīlārṇava, and the satirical Kaliviḍambana; his role in the Śrīvidyā and Advaita traditions in South India is represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Purandaradāsa
teacher.description: Purandaradāsa (1484–1564), the 'father of Carnatic music' (Karnataka Sangeeta Pitamaha), composer of 475,000+ kīrtanas in Kannada and Sanskrit; his systematization of music pedagogy (sarali, janta, alankara, geetam, swarajati, varnam), his devotion to Viṭṭhala, and his role in the Haridāsa movement are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Purandaradāsa (1484–1564), the 'father of Carnatic music' (Karnataka Sangeeta Pitamaha), composer of 475,000+ kīrtanas in Kannada and Sanskrit; his systematization of music pedagogy (sarali, janta, alankara, geetam, swarajati, varnam), his devotion to Viṭṭhala, and his role in the Haridāsa movement are represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Rāghavendra Svāmī
teacher.description: Rāghavendra Svāmī (1595–1671), the Dvaita Vedānta pontiff (Rāghavendra Maṭha, Mantralayam), known for his commentaries on Madhva's works and his reputation as a miracle-worker; his role in the Dvaita tradition, the Brindavan at Mantralayam, and his continued popular veneration are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Rāghavendra Svāmī (1595–1671), the Dvaita Vedānta pontiff (Rāghavendra Maṭha, Mantralayam), known for his commentaries on Madhva's works and his reputation as a miracle-worker; his role in the Dvaita tradition, the Brindavan at Mantralayam, and his continued popular veneration are represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṃsa
teacher.description: Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṃsa (1836–1886), the 19th-century mystic of Dakṣiṇeśvar, devotee of Kālī, who experienced diverse religious paths (Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, Advaita, Islam, Christianity) and declared 'yato mat tato patha' (as many paths, so many ways); his disciple Vivekananda, the Ramakrishna Mission, and his universalist message are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṃsa (1836–1886), the 19th-century mystic of Dakṣiṇeśvar, devotee of Kālī, who experienced diverse religious paths (Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, Advaita, Islam, Christianity) and declared 'yato mat tato patha' (as many paths, so many ways); his disciple Vivekananda, the Ramakrishna Mission, and his universalist message are represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Rāmānanda
teacher.description: Rāmānanda (c. 14th–15th century), the founder of the Rāmānandī sect, a North Indian Vaiṣṇava tradition emphasizing Rāma-bhakti and the accessibility of devotion regardless of caste; his disciples included Kabīr, Ravidās, and Sena; his role in the Bhakti movement in North India is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Rāmānanda (c. 14th–15th century), the founder of the Rāmānandī sect, a North Indian Vaiṣṇava tradition emphasizing Rāma-bhakti and the accessibility of devotion regardless of caste; his disciples included Kabīr, Ravidās, and Sena; his role in the Bhakti movement in North India is represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Śyāma Śāstri
teacher.description: Śyāma Śāstri (1762–1827), one of the Carnatic trinity, composer of ~300 kṛtis in Telugu and Sanskrit, known for his swarajatis, his kamakshi navaratna mālikā, his ananda bhairavi compositions, and his distinctive rhythmic structures (tāḷa); his influence on Carnatic music is represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Śyāma Śāstri (1762–1827), one of the Carnatic trinity, composer of ~300 kṛtis in Telugu and Sanskrit, known for his swarajatis, his kamakshi navaratna mālikā, his ananda bhairavi compositions, and his distinctive rhythmic structures (tāḷa); his influence on Carnatic music is represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Śrī Aurobindo
teacher.description: Śrī Aurobindo (1872–1950), the nationalist, philosopher, and yogi who developed Integral Yoga (Pūrṇa Yoga); his works (The Life Divine, Synthesis of Yoga, Savitri), his concept of the Supermind, the descent of consciousness, the Ashram at Pondicherry, and the Auroville township are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Śrī Aurobindo (1872–1950), the nationalist, philosopher, and yogi who developed Integral Yoga (Pūrṇa Yoga); his works (The Life Divine, Synthesis of Yoga, Savitri), his concept of the Supermind, the descent of consciousness, the Ashram at Pondicherry, and the Auroville township are represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Sūrdās
teacher.description: Sūrdās (c. 1478–1583), the blind poet-saint of the Puṣṭimārga (Vallabha sect), composer of the Sūrsāgar (thousands of Braj bhāṣā poems on Kṛṣṇa-līlā); his depiction of Kṛṣṇa's childhood (bāla-līlā), the gopīs' love, and the philosophy of puṣṭi (grace) are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Sūrdās (c. 1478–1583), the blind poet-saint of the Puṣṭimārga (Vallabha sect), composer of the Sūrsāgar (thousands of Braj bhāṣā poems on Kṛṣṇa-līlā); his depiction of Kṛṣṇa's childhood (bāla-līlā), the gopīs' love, and the philosophy of puṣṭi (grace) are represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Tulsīdās
teacher.description: Tulsīdās (1532–1623), the composer of the Rāmacaritamānasa (Awadhi retelling of the Rāmāyaṇa), the Hanumān Cālīsā, and the Vinaya Patrikā; his role in popularizing Rāma-bhakti in North India, his founding of the Sankat Mochan Temple (Varanasi), and his influence on the Rāmānandī tradition are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Tulsīdās (1532–1623), the composer of the Rāmacaritamānasa (Awadhi retelling of the Rāmāyaṇa), the Hanumān Cālīsā, and the Vinaya Patrikā; his role in popularizing Rāma-bhakti in North India, his founding of the Sankat Mochan Temple (Varanasi), and his influence on the Rāmānandī tradition are represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Tyāgarāja
teacher.description: Tyāgarāja (1767–1847), one of the Carnatic trinity, composer of ~24,000 kṛtis in Telugu and Sanskrit, mostly on Rāma; his pancharatna kṛtis, his devotion to Rāma, his life in Tiruvaiyaru, and his influence on Carnatic music pedagogy are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Tyāgarāja (1767–1847), one of the Carnatic trinity, composer of ~24,000 kṛtis in Telugu and Sanskrit, mostly on Rāma; his pancharatna kṛtis, his devotion to Rāma, his life in Tiruvaiyaru, and his influence on Carnatic music pedagogy are represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Vālmīki
teacher.description: Traditional attribution identifies Vālmīki as the author of the Rāmāyaṇa; traditional attribution and historical biography are kept distinct in this record.
teacher.body: Traditional attribution identifies Vālmīki as the author of the Rāmāyaṇa; traditional attribution and historical biography are kept distinct in this record.

teacher.title: Swami Vivekananda
teacher.description: Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902), the chief disciple of Rāmakṛṣṇa, the founder of the Ramakrishna Mission, the exponent of practical Vedānta at the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions (Chicago); his synthesis of Advaita with social service, his call for 'man-making education', and his role in modern Hindu renaissance are represented here as a catalogue entry. ---
teacher.body:
Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902), the chief disciple of Rāmakṛṣṇa, the founder of the Ramakrishna Mission, the exponent of practical Vedānta at the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions (Chicago); his synthesis of Advaita with social service, his call for 'man-making education', and his role in modern Hindu renaissance are represented here as a catalogue entry.
---

teacher.title: Vyāsa
teacher.description: Traditional attribution identifies Vyāsa as the compiler of the Vedas and author of the Mahābhārata; traditional attribution is not presented as modern historical certainty.
teacher.body: Traditional attribution identifies Vyāsa as the compiler of the Vedas and author of the Mahābhārata; traditional attribution is not presented as modern historical certainty.

acharya.title: Caitanya Mahāprabhu
acharya.description: A 15th–16th century Bengali saint and ācārya, founder of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition; traditional hagiography and historical scholarship are kept distinct.
acharya.body: A 15th–16th century Bengali saint and ācārya, founder of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition; traditional hagiography and historical scholarship are kept distinct.

acharya.title: Jīva Gosvāmī
acharya.description: A 16th-century Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theologian, author of the Ṣaṭ-sandarbha and systematic expositor of Caitanya's teachings; traditional attribution is represented without historical conflation.
acharya.body: A 16th-century Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theologian, author of the Ṣaṭ-sandarbha and systematic expositor of Caitanya's teachings; traditional attribution is represented without historical conflation.

acharya.title: Madhva
acharya.description: Traditional dating assigns Madhva to the 13th century CE; scholarly dates vary. He is associated with Dvaita Vedānta through traditional and textual lineages; this record represents his tradition without ranking it against other schools.
acharya.body: Traditional dating assigns Madhva to the 13th century CE; scholarly dates vary. He is associated with Dvaita Vedānta through traditional and textual lineages; this record represents his tradition without ranking it against other schools.

acharya.title: Nimbārka
acharya.description: A Vedānta ācārya traditionally associated with Dvaitādvaita (Bhedābheda) Vedānta; traditional dating and biography are kept distinct from historical scholarship.
acharya.body: A Vedānta ācārya traditionally associated with Dvaitādvaita (Bhedābheda) Vedānta; traditional dating and biography are kept distinct from historical scholarship.

acharya.title: Rāmānuja
acharya.description: Traditional dating assigns Rāmānuja to the 11th–12th century CE; scholarly dates vary. He is associated with Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta through traditional and textual lineages; this record represents his tradition without ranking it against other schools.
acharya.body: Traditional dating assigns Rāmānuja to the 11th–12th century CE; scholarly dates vary. He is associated with Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta through traditional and textual lineages; this record represents his tradition without ranking it against other schools.

acharya.title: Śaṅkara
acharya.description: Traditional attribution places Śaṅkara in the 8th century CE; scholarly dating varies and historical reconstruction remains distinct from hagiographical accounts. He is associated with Advaita Vedānta through traditional and textual lineages.
acharya.body: Traditional attribution places Śaṅkara in the 8th century CE; scholarly dating varies and historical reconstruction remains distinct from hagiographical accounts. He is associated with Advaita Vedānta through traditional and textual lineages.

acharya.title: Vallabha
acharya.description: A Vedānta ācārya associated with Śuddhādvaita (Pure Non-dualism) and the Puṣṭimārga tradition; traditional dating and biography are kept distinct from historical scholarship.
acharya.body: A Vedānta ācārya associated with Śuddhādvaita (Pure Non-dualism) and the Puṣṭimārga tradition; traditional dating and biography are kept distinct from historical scholarship.

philosophical-school.title: Advaita Vedānta
philosophical-school.description: A Vedānta tradition represented separately from Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita, with its own textual and interpretive history.
philosophical-school.body: A Vedānta tradition represented separately from Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita, with its own textual and interpretive history.

philosophical-school.title: Dvaita Vedānta
philosophical-school.description: A distinct Vedānta tradition represented without ranking it against other schools.
philosophical-school.body: A distinct Vedānta tradition represented without ranking it against other schools.

philosophical-school.title: Nyāya
philosophical-school.description: A philosophical tradition focused on logic, epistemology, and the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), with a distinct technical vocabulary.
philosophical-school.body: A philosophical tradition focused on logic, epistemology, and the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), with a distinct technical vocabulary.

philosophical-school.title: Pūrvamīmāṃsā
philosophical-school.description: A tradition focused on Vedic hermeneutics, ritual action, and the authority of the Veda as an instrument of valid knowledge.
philosophical-school.body: A tradition focused on Vedic hermeneutics, ritual action, and the authority of the Veda as an instrument of valid knowledge.

philosophical-school.title: Sāṃkhya
philosophical-school.description: A dualistic philosophical tradition distinguishing puruṣa and prakṛti, represented here without reducing its technical categories to a universal summary.
philosophical-school.body: A dualistic philosophical tradition distinguishing puruṣa and prakṛti, represented here without reducing its technical categories to a universal summary.

philosophical-school.title: Vaiśeṣika
philosophical-school.description: A school of atomistic metaphysics and category theory, closely associated with Nyāya in later synthetic developments.
philosophical-school.body: A school of atomistic metaphysics and category theory, closely associated with Nyāya in later synthetic developments.

philosophical-school.title: Vedānta
philosophical-school.description: A family of traditions interpreting the Upaniṣads, Brahma-sūtras, and Bhagavad Gītā; its internal schools are represented separately.
philosophical-school.body: A family of traditions interpreting the Upaniṣads, Brahma-sūtras, and Bhagavad Gītā; its internal schools are represented separately.

philosophical-school.title: Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta
philosophical-school.description: A distinct Vedānta tradition represented with attention to its own interpretations and lineage contexts.
philosophical-school.body: A distinct Vedānta tradition represented with attention to its own interpretations and lineage contexts.

philosophical-school.title: Yoga Darśana
philosophical-school.description: The philosophical school systematized in the Yogasūtras, distinct from the many modern and traditional uses of the term yoga.
philosophical-school.body: The philosophical school systematized in the Yogasūtras, distinct from the many modern and traditional uses of the term yoga.

practice.title: Abhiṣeka
practice.description: The ritual bathing of a deity or sacred object with water, milk, curd, honey, etc.; its materials, mantras, and occasions vary by tradition and Āgama.
practice.body: The ritual bathing of a deity or sacred object with water, milk, curd, honey, etc.; its materials, mantras, and occasions vary by tradition and Āgama.

practice.title: Ārati
practice.description: The waving of lights before a deity as the culminating offering in worship; its form, number of lamps, and accompanying hymns vary by tradition.
practice.body: The waving of lights before a deity as the culminating offering in worship; its form, number of lamps, and accompanying hymns vary by tradition.

practice.title: Arcana
practice.description: The ritual worship of a deity through sequential offerings (upacāras), typically in temple or home shrine; its sequence and items vary by tradition.
practice.body: The ritual worship of a deity through sequential offerings (upacāras), typically in temple or home shrine; its sequence and items vary by tradition.

practice.title: Bhajan
practice.description: A devotional song or hymn, often in vernacular languages, sung individually or in groups; its forms, languages, and musical styles are diverse across regions and traditions.
practice.body: A devotional song or hymn, often in vernacular languages, sung individually or in groups; its forms, languages, and musical styles are diverse across regions and traditions.

practice.title: Dhyāna
practice.description: A contemplative practice term whose methods and aims vary across philosophical and living traditions.
practice.body: A contemplative practice term whose methods and aims vary across philosophical and living traditions.

practice.title: Havana
practice.description: Synonym for homa, the fire offering ritual; represented here as a catalogue entry without duplicating the homa record.
practice.body: Synonym for homa, the fire offering ritual; represented here as a catalogue entry without duplicating the homa record.

practice.title: Homa
practice.description: The fire offering (homa/havana) in which oblations are poured into the sacred fire; its mantras, materials, and purposes vary by Vedic school and occasion.
practice.body: The fire offering (homa/havana) in which oblations are poured into the sacred fire; its mantras, materials, and purposes vary by Vedic school and occasion.

practice.title: Japa
practice.description: A practice category involving repeated recitation in varied contexts; traditions differ in mantra, method and guidance.
practice.body: A practice category involving repeated recitation in varied contexts; traditions differ in mantra, method and guidance.

practice.title: Kīrtana
practice.description: A form of devotional call-and-response singing, often accompanied by instruments; its structure, repertoire, and performance contexts vary across traditions and regions.
practice.body: A form of devotional call-and-response singing, often accompanied by instruments; its structure, repertoire, and performance contexts vary across traditions and regions.

practice.title: Nāma Saṅkīrtana
practice.description: The congregational chanting of divine names, central to many bhakti traditions; its forms, melodies, and organizational structures vary widely.
practice.body: The congregational chanting of divine names, central to many bhakti traditions; its forms, melodies, and organizational structures vary widely.

practice.title: Pañcāmṛta
practice.description: The "five nectars" (milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar) mixed as a ritual offering and later distributed as prasāda; proportions and additional ingredients vary regionally.
practice.body: The "five nectars" (milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar) mixed as a ritual offering and later distributed as prasāda; proportions and additional ingredients vary regionally.

practice.title: Prāṇa Pratiṣṭhā
practice.description: The ritual installation of the life-force (prāṇa) into a temple image (mūrti), transforming it into a living embodiment of the deity; its elaborate procedures vary by Āgama tradition.
practice.body: The ritual installation of the life-force (prāṇa) into a temple image (mūrti), transforming it into a living embodiment of the deity; its elaborate procedures vary by Āgama tradition.

practice.title: Pravacana
practice.description: A scriptural discourse or sermon, traditionally delivered by a learned teacher; its content, language, and setting vary across traditions and audiences.
practice.body: A scriptural discourse or sermon, traditionally delivered by a learned teacher; its content, language, and setting vary across traditions and audiences.

practice.title: Pūjā
practice.description: A broad practice category whose forms, meanings and procedures vary by tradition, place and community. This portal does not provide universal ritual instructions here.
practice.body: A broad practice category whose forms, meanings and procedures vary by tradition, place and community. This portal does not provide universal ritual instructions here.

practice.title: Sandhyāvandana
practice.description: A daily observance associated with the junctures of the day, whose specific mantras and procedures differ by Vedic school and family tradition.
practice.body: A daily observance associated with the junctures of the day, whose specific mantras and procedures differ by Vedic school and family tradition.

practice.title: Ṣoḍaśopacāra
practice.description: The "sixteen offerings" (upacāras) in formal deity worship: invocation, seat, water, etc.; the exact list and sequence vary by tradition and Āgama.
practice.body: The "sixteen offerings" (upacāras) in formal deity worship: invocation, seat, water, etc.; the exact list and sequence vary by tradition and Āgama.

practice.title: Svādhyāya
practice.description: The practice of self-study or recitation of one's Vedic branch; a niyama in Yoga philosophy and a daily duty in Dharmaśāstra traditions.
practice.body: The practice of self-study or recitation of one's Vedic branch; a niyama in Yoga philosophy and a daily duty in Dharmaśāstra traditions.

practice.title: Tapas
practice.description: A term for austerity, heat, or disciplined effort whose forms and purposes vary across Vedic, Yoga, and Purāṇic contexts.
practice.body: A term for austerity, heat, or disciplined effort whose forms and purposes vary across Vedic, Yoga, and Purāṇic contexts.

practice.title: Tīrtha and pilgrimage
practice.description: A category for pilgrimage and sacred journeys whose meanings and practices vary by place and tradition.
practice.body: A category for pilgrimage and sacred journeys whose meanings and practices vary by place and tradition.

practice.title: Vrata
practice.description: A category of vows or observances whose forms and meanings vary by region, text and tradition.
practice.body: A category of vows or observances whose forms and meanings vary by region, text and tradition.

ritual.title: Annaprāśana
ritual.description: The seventh saṃskāra, the first feeding of solid food, typically in the sixth month; its timing and food items vary by tradition.
ritual.body: The seventh saṃskāra, the first feeding of solid food, typically in the sixth month; its timing and food items vary by tradition.

ritual.title: Antyeṣṭi
ritual.description: The final sacrament or funeral rites, whose procedures and underlying eschatology differ across texts, regions, and communities.
ritual.body: The final sacrament or funeral rites, whose procedures and underlying eschatology differ across texts, regions, and communities.

ritual.title: Cūḍākaraṇa
ritual.description: The eighth saṃskāra, the first haircut (tonsure), typically in the first or third year; its timing and rites vary by text and regional tradition.
ritual.body: The eighth saṃskāra, the first haircut (tonsure), typically in the first or third year; its timing and rites vary by text and regional tradition.

ritual.title: Garbhādhāna
ritual.description: The first saṃskāra, the rite of conception or impregnation, prescribed in Dharmaśātra for the desire of progeny; its observance varies by text and tradition.
ritual.body: The first saṃskāra, the rite of conception or impregnation, prescribed in Dharmaśātra for the desire of progeny; its observance varies by text and tradition.

ritual.title: Jātakarma
ritual.description: The fourth saṃskāra, the birth rite performed immediately after delivery; its mantras and procedures vary across texts and family traditions.
ritual.body: The fourth saṃskāra, the birth rite performed immediately after delivery; its mantras and procedures vary across texts and family traditions.

ritual.title: Karṇavedha
ritual.description: The ninth saṃskāra, the ear-piercing rite; its timing, method, and gender applicability vary across texts and regional customs.
ritual.body: The ninth saṃskāra, the ear-piercing rite; its timing, method, and gender applicability vary across texts and regional customs.

ritual.title: Nāmakaraṇa
ritual.description: The fifth saṃskāra, the naming ceremony typically performed on the eleventh or twelfth day after birth; its timing and customs vary regionally.
ritual.body: The fifth saṃskāra, the naming ceremony typically performed on the eleventh or twelfth day after birth; its timing and customs vary regionally.

ritual.title: Niṣkramaṇa
ritual.description: The sixth saṃskāra, the first outing of the child, traditionally in the fourth month; its observance varies by text and family custom.
ritual.body: The sixth saṃskāra, the first outing of the child, traditionally in the fourth month; its observance varies by text and family custom.

ritual.title: Pañca Mahāyajña
ritual.description: The five great daily sacrifices—devayajña, ṛṣiyajña, pitṛyajña, bhūtayajña, manusyayajña—prescribed in Dharmaśāstra for householders.
ritual.body: The five great daily sacrifices—devayajña, ṛṣiyajña, pitṛyajña, bhūtayajña, manusyayajña—prescribed in Dharmaśāstra for householders.

ritual.title: Puṃsavana
ritual.description: The second saṃskāra, performed during pregnancy for the well-being of the fetus; its timing and procedure vary across Dharmaśāstra texts.
ritual.body: The second saṃskāra, performed during pregnancy for the well-being of the fetus; its timing and procedure vary across Dharmaśāstra texts.

ritual.title: Samāvartana
ritual.description: The eleventh saṃskāra, the completion of Vedic studentship and return home; its observance marks the transition from brahmacarya to gṛhastha.
ritual.body: The eleventh saṃskāra, the completion of Vedic studentship and return home; its observance marks the transition from brahmacarya to gṛhastha.

ritual.title: Saṃskāra
ritual.description: The sacraments or rites of passage marking life transitions, whose number, sequence, and content vary across textual and regional traditions.
ritual.body: The sacraments or rites of passage marking life transitions, whose number, sequence, and content vary across textual and regional traditions.

ritual.title: Śrāddha
ritual.description: The ancestral offering rites whose procedures, timing, and eligibility vary across textual prescriptions and regional practices.
ritual.body: The ancestral offering rites whose procedures, timing, and eligibility vary across textual prescriptions and regional practices.

ritual.title: Sīmantonnayana
ritual.description: The third saṃskāra, the parting of the hair rite performed during late pregnancy; its observance varies by text and regional tradition.
ritual.body: The third saṃskāra, the parting of the hair rite performed during late pregnancy; its observance varies by text and regional tradition.

ritual.title: Upanayana
ritual.description: The initiation ceremony conferring Vedic studentship, whose age, rites, and social applicability differ across textual and community contexts.
ritual.body: The initiation ceremony conferring Vedic studentship, whose age, rites, and social applicability differ across textual and community contexts.

ritual.title: Vidyārambha
ritual.description: The tenth saṃskāra, the commencement of formal education, often coinciding with upanayana or performed separately; its rites vary by tradition.
ritual.body: The tenth saṃskāra, the commencement of formal education, often coinciding with upanayana or performed separately; its rites vary by tradition.

ritual.title: Vivāha
ritual.description: The marriage sacrament whose rituals, mantras, and legal frameworks vary across textual prescriptions and regional customary practices.
ritual.body: The marriage sacrament whose rituals, mantras, and legal frameworks vary across textual prescriptions and regional customary practices.

ritual.title: Yajña
ritual.description: A ritual category with different textual, historical and contemporary contexts; this portal does not provide universal performance instructions.

scripture.title: Agni Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Agni Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in approximately 383 chapters, transmitted as a discourse of Agni to the sage Vasiṣṭha. Its encyclopedic scope covers cosmology (sarga, pratisarga), geography (dvīpa, varṣa), temple architecture and iconography (pratimā-lakṣaṇa), medicine (Āyurveda), polity (rāja-dharma), Dharmaśāstra topics (saṃskāras, vrata, dāna), and yoga. It preserves the Lakṣmī-kalpa and the Śiva-rātra sections. A key source for traditional Indian knowledge systems. ---

scripture.description: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad Bhāgavatam), one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in twelve skandhas (books) and ~18,000 verses. Composed as a dialogue between Śuka and King Parīkṣit on the banks of the Gaṅgā. Skandha 1-2: creation, cosmology, and the avatāras; Skandha 3-4: Kapila's Sāṅkhya, Dhruva, Prahlāda; Skandha 5: Bharata, Ṛṣabha, cosmic geography; Skandha 6: Ajāmila, Vaivasvata, Nṛsiṃha; Skandha 7: Prahlāda, Nṛsiṃha; Skandha 8: Vāmana, churning of the ocean; Skandha 9: genealogies; Skandha 10: Kṛṣṇa's līlā (Vṛndāvana, Mathurā, Dvārakā); Skandha 11: Uddhava-gītā, Yadu dynasty; Skandha 12: future, Kali age, Māhātmya. Central to Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism and bhakti traditions across India. ---

scripture.title: Bhaviṣya Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in four parts (Brāhma, Madhyama, Pratisarga, Uttara) and ~28,000 verses, narrated by Sūta to the sages at Naimiṣāraṇya. Known for its "future" (bhaviṣya) orientation — prophecies, royal genealogies of future dynasties (Maurya, Gupta, Harsha, medieval Indian rulers, and even British period references), the Sūrya-vaṃśa and Candra-vaṃśa lineages, the Sāyaṇācārya's solar worship, the Kṛṣṇa-līlā, the Tulasī-māhātmya, the Rāma-nāma-māhātmya, the Kāśī-māhātmya, the Gayā-śrāddha, and numerous vrata-kathās. The only Purāṇa with extensive historical/prophetic content on post-Vedic Indian dynasties. Controversial for its late interpolations; the Pratisargaparvan is considered a later addition. ---

scripture.title: Brahma Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Brahma Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in ~10,000 verses, traditionally ascribed to Brahmā and narrated to the sages at Naimiṣāraṇya. Covers creation (sarga), the solar and lunar dynasties, the geography of Bhārata-varṣa, the seven dvīpas, the glory of the Godāvarī and other rivers, the Śiva and Viṣṇu kṣetras (Ekāmra, Purī, Koṇārka, Kāśī), the Purī Jagannātha temple, the Ratha-yātrā, and the Saura and Gāṇapatya traditions. Contains the Gautamī-māhātmya (Godāvarī pilgrimage) and the Koṇārka-māhātmya. Bridges Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and Saura traditions; especially important for Odisha and Andhra temple mythology. ---

scripture.title: Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in four parts (prakriyā, anuṣaṅga, upodghāta, upasaṃhāra) and ~12,000 verses. Details the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), creation cycles, geography of the seven dvīpas, the Aṣṭādaśa-śakti-pīṭhas (eighteen Goddess shrines), and the Lalitopākhyāna (narrative of Lalitā Tripurasundarī) in the Uttarārdha. Contains the Āditya-hṛdaya, the Navagraha-stotras, and detailed pilgrimage (tīrtha) sections for Kāñcī, Śrīśaila, and other Śākta sites. Closely related to the Vāyu Purāṇa; together they preserve the Āditya and Śaiva-Śākta cosmologies. Key for Śākta tradition and South Indian temple mythology. ---

scripture.title: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrī Devī Bhāgavatam), a major Śākta Mahāpurāṇa in 12 skandhas and ~18,000 verses, modeled on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa's structure but centered on the Goddess. Skandha 1: creation, the Goddess as śakti; Skandha 2-3: the Devī's forms, the battle with Mahiṣāsura; Skandha 4: the Devī-gītā (the Goddess's teaching on jñāna, yoga, bhakti); Skandha 5: the Śākta cosmology, the Śrī-cakra, the nine nityās; Skandha 6: the Kālī-krama, the ten Mahāvidyās; Skandha 7: the Navarātrī vrata, the Caṇḍī-pāṭha procedure; Skandha 8-9: the glories of Śākta pīṭhas (Kāmākhyā, Kālikā, Tārāpīṭha); Skandha 10-11: the Rāma and Kṛṣṇa narratives retold from the Śākta perspective; Skandha 12: liberation through Devī-bhakti. The primary text for the Devī-gītā and Śākta theology, influential in Bengal and Assam. --- A major Śākta Purāṇa centered on the Goddess; represented here as a catalogue entry without reproducing translations.

scripture.title: Garuḍa Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Garuḍa Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in ~19,000 verses, narrated by Garuḍa to Kaśyapa (or Viṣṇu to Garuḍa). Two main parts: Pūrvakhanda (Ācāra-kāṇḍa, Dharma-kāṇḍa, Preta-kāṇḍa) and Uttarakhanda (Brahma-kāṇḍa). Covers Viṣṇu worship, saṃskāras, vrata, dāna, temple construction, iconography, gemology (ratna-śāstra), astrology, medicine (Āyurveda), the afterlife journey (pretakalpā), the realms of Yama, funeral rites (antyeṣṭi), śrāddha, and the path to liberation through Viṣṇu-bhakti. Authoritative for death rituals and śrāddha procedures across Hindu traditions. ---

scripture.title: Kūrma Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Kūrma Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in two parts (Pūrvabhāga and Uttarabhāga) and ~17,000 verses, narrated by Kūrma (Viṣṇu's tortoise avatar) to the sages at Naimiṣāraṇya. Pūrvabhāga: creation, the four puruṣārthas (dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa), the glory of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-hṛdaya, the unity of Śiva and Viṣṇu, the ṛṣi genealogies; Uttarabhāga: the Īśvara-gītā (Śiva's teaching on yoga and jñāna), the Vyāsa-gītā, the Śiva-gītā, pilgrimage to Kāśī, Prayāga, Gayā, and the Śiva kṣetras. A synthesis text emphasizing Śiva-Viṣṇu non-difference (abheda) and the yoga of knowledge and devotion. ---

scripture.title: Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in 137 chapters and ~9,000 verses, narrated as a dialogue between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and Jaimini. Chapters 1-42: cosmology, creation, genealogies, the manvantaras; Chapters 43-80: the glory of the Sun (Sūrya), the legend of King Harishchandra; Chapters 81-93: the Devī Māhātmya (Durgā Saptashatī / Caṇḍī-pāṭha) — the Goddess's battles against Madhu-Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣāsura, and Śumbha-Niśumbha, the foundation of Śākta worship and Navarātrī; Chapters 94-137: the story of Dama, the glories of the Goddess, liberation through Devī-bhakti. The primary textual source for the Caṇḍī-pāṭha recited during Durgā Pūjā and Navarātrī across India, especially Bengal. ---

scripture.title: Matsya Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Matsya Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in ~14,000 verses and 291 chapters, narrated by Matsya (Viṣṇu's fish avatar) to Manu. Covers the Matsya avatāra and the flood legend, the seven Manus, royal genealogies (Sūryavaṃśa, Candravaṃśa), the five characteristics of a Purāṇa (pañca-lakṣaṇa), temple architecture (vāstu-śāstra: prāsāda, maṇḍapa, gopura, pratimā-lakṣaṇa), iconography of major deities, vrata rituals (Śivarātri, Caturmāsya, Ekādaśī), the Śrāddha-vidhi, the Prayāga-māhātmya, the Kāśī-māhātmya, and the Narmadā-māhātmya. The earliest Purāṇic source for Hindu temple architecture and iconography. ---

scripture.description: The Nṛsiṃha Upapurāṇa is one of the eighteen Upapurāṇas, focusing on the Nṛsiṃha (man-lion) avatar of Viṣṇu. It contains stories of the devotee Prahlāda, the defeat of the demon Hiraṇyakaipu, and the symbolism of the Nṛsiṃha form as the Supreme Being who transcends all categories. The text also includes a description of the iconography, the sacred places associated with Nṛsiṃha worship, and the theological significance of the avatar. It is associated with the Vaiṣṇava tradition and is recited during the monthly Nṛsiṃha-vātaṇa and the annual Nṛsiṃha-jayantī festival. --- A subsidiary Purāṇa focusing on the Narasiṃha avatar, recited in Vaiṣṇava temples and household practice.

Organized around the lotus (padma) cosmology. Sṛṣṭi-khaṇḍa: creation, the glory of Puṣkara and other tīrthas; Bhūmi-khaṇḍa: earth geography, rivers, mountains, the Bhārata-varṣa; Svarga-khaṇḍa: heavens, the story of Rāma (Rāmāyaṇa summary), the glory of Ekādaśī; Pātāla-khaṇḍa: netherworlds, the story of Śeṣa, Viṣṇu's yoga-nidrā; Uttara-khaṇḍa: the essence of bhakti, the glory of Viṣṇu's names (Viṣṇu-sahasranāma context), pilgrimage to Brahmāvarta, Kāśī, Prayāga; Kriyā-yoga-khaṇḍa: temple rituals, vrata, dāna, the Puruṣottama-māhātmya (Jagannātha). Major source for tīrtha-māhātmya and Vaiṣṇava ritual. --- One of the largest Mahāpurāṇas, organized around the lotus (padma) cosmology with extensive pilgrimage and ritual sections; represented here as a catalogue entry.

scripture.title: Śiva Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Śiva Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in seven saṃhitās (Vidyeśvara, Rudra, Śatarudra, Koṭirudra, Umā, Kailāsa, Vāyavīya) and ~24,000 verses. Saṃhitā 1 (Vidyeśvara): glory of Śiva, liṅga worship, jyotirliṅgas; Saṃhitā 2 (Rudra): Rudra's forms, the eleven Rudras; Saṃhitā 3 (Śatarudra): hundred names of Rudra, Śiva's cosmic dance; Saṃhitā 4 (Koṭirudra): twelve jyotirliṅgas (Somnath, Mallikārjuna, Mahākāleśvara, Omkāreśvara, Kedārnāth, Bhīmaśaṅkar, Viśvanāth, Tryambakeśvara, Vaidyanāth, Nāgeśvara, Rāmeśvara, Ghṛṣṇeśvara); Saṃhitā 5 (Umā): Pārvatī's birth, marriage, Gaṇeśa, Skanda; Saṃhitā 6 (Kailāsa): Kailāsa, the yoga of Śiva, the five faces; Saṃhitā 7 (Vāyavīya): Vāyu's narration, the Śiva-gītā, liberation through Śiva-bhakti. Central to Śaiva Siddhānta and temple traditions. ---
scripture.body:
The Śiva Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in seven saṃhitās (Vidyeśvara, Rudra, Śatarudra, Koṭirudra, Umā, Kailāsa, Vāyavīya) and ~24,000 verses. Saṃhitā 1 (Vidyeśvara): glory of Śiva, liṅga worship, jyotirliṅgas; Saṃhitā 2 (Rudra): Rudra's forms, the eleven Rudras; Saṃhitā 3 (Śatarudra): hundred names of Rudra, Śiva's cosmic dance; Saṃhitā 4 (Koṭirudra): twelve jyotirliṅgas (Somnath, Mallikārjuna, Mahākāleśvara, Omkāreśvara, Kedārnāth, Bhīmaśaṅkar, Viśvanāth, Tryambakeśvara, Vaidyanāth, Nāgeśvara, Rāmeśvara, Ghṛṣṇeśvara); Saṃhitā 5 (Umā): Pārvatī's birth, marriage, Gaṇeśa, Skanda; Saṃhitā 6 (Kailāsa): Kailāsa, the yoga of Śiva, the five faces; Saṃhitā 7 (Vāyavīya): Vāyu's narration, the Śiva-gītā, liberation through Śiva-bhakti. scripture.title: Skanda Purāṇa
aliases: ச கந ட ப ர ணம்
scripture.description: The Skanda Purāṇa, the largest Mahāpurāṇa at ~81,000+ verses in seven khaṇḍas (Māheśvara, Viṣṇu, Brahma, Kāśī, Āvantya, Nāgara, Prabhāsa). Māheśvara-khaṇḍa: Śiva's glory, the twelve jyotirliṅgas, Kedāra-khaṇḍa (Himalayan tīrthas); Viṣṇu-khaṇḍa: Viṣṇu avatāras, Badarī, Puruṣottama (Jagannātha); Brahma-khaṇḍa: creation, Brahmā's life, Puṣkara, Gayā; Kāśī-khaṇḍa: Kāśī/Avimiukta, the glory of Kāśī, the Annapūrṇā temple; Āvantya-khaṇḍa: Avantī/Ujjayinī, Mahākāleśvara, the Siṃhastha Kumbha; Nāgara-khaṇḍa: Gujarat tīrthas, Dvārakā, Prabhāsa; Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa: Somnāth, the Yādava dynasty, the end of Kṛṣṇa's līlā. The definitive tīrtha-māhātmya text for Śaiva and pan-Hindu pilgrimage. ---
scripture.body:
The Skanda Purāṇa, the largest Mahāpurāṇa at ~81,000+ verses in seven khaṇḍas (Māheśvara, Viṣṇu, Brahma, Kāśī, Āvantya, Nāgara, Prabhāsa). Māheśvara-khaṇḍa: Śiva's glory, the twelve jyotirliṅgas, Kedāra-khaṇḍa (Himalayan tīrthas); Viṣṇu-khaṇḍa: Viṣṇu avatāras, Badarī, Puruṣottama (Jagannātha); Brahma-khaṇḍa: creation, Brahmā's life, Puṣkara, Gayā; Kāśī-khaṇḍa: Kāśī/Avimiukta, the glory of Kāśī, the Annapūrṇā temple; Āvantya-khaṇḍa: Avantī/Ujjayinī, Mahākāleśvara, the Siṃhastha Kumbha; Nāgara-khaṇḍa: Gujarat tīrthas, Dvārakā, Prabhāsa; Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa: Somnāth, the Yādava dynasty, the end of Kṛṣṇa's līlā. The definitive tīrtha-māhātmya text for Śaiva and pan-Hindu pilgrimage.

A key text for Kurukṣetra pilgrimage and the Vāmana-Nṛsiṃha dual focus of Viṣṇu worship. ---

Closely related to the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa (shares the Lalitopākhyāna and Āditya-hṛdaya). Preserves the early Śaiva cosmology and the genealogical tradition of the Purāṇas. ---

scripture.title: Viṣṇu Purāṇa
scripture.description: The Viṣṇu Purāṇa, one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas in six aṃśas (parts) and ~23,000 verses, attributed to Parāśara and narrated to Maitreya. Aṃśa 1: creation (sarga), cosmology, the varṇāśrama system; Aṃśa 2: geography (dvīpas, varṣas), Pātāla, hells, the seven dvīpas; Aṃśa 3: Manus, manvantaras, the solar and lunar dynasties (Sūryavaṃśa, Candravaṃśa); Aṃśa 4: detailed genealogies of kings through the ages; Aṃśa 5: Kṛṣṇa's life (Mathurā, Vṛndāvana, Dvārakā, Jarāsandha, Kālayavana, the Pāṇḍavas); Aṃśa 6: dissolution (pralaya), the path of liberation, the glories of Viṣṇu-bhakti. The earliest and most systematic Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, foundational for later bhakti traditions. ---

temple.title: Ahobilam Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Nava Narasiṃha Temple complex at Ahobilam (Nandyal district, Andhra Pradesh), a Divya Deśam with nine shrines for the nine forms of Narasiṃha (Nava Narasiṃha): Ahobila, Bhārgava, Yogananda, Chatravata, Krodha, Malola, Jvālā, Pavana, and Karanja. Spread across the Nallamala Hills. Glorified by Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār and Nammāḻvār. The annual Brahmotsavam and the Narasiṃha-jayantī attract thousands. Unique for the nine distinct Narasiṃha forms in one pilgrimage circuit. ---

temple.description: The Aṣṭabhujākaram Temple (Eight-armed Viṣṇu) at Kāñcīpuram (Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu with eight arms (aṣṭa-bhuja) holding the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, arrow, sword, and shield. The Cōḷa-period temple where Viṣṇu appeared to the sage Bhṛgu. Glorified by Poygai Āḻvār, Bhūta Āḻvār, Pēy Āḻvār, and Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The annual Brahmotsavam and the Bhṛgu-pūjā are celebrated. temple.title: Badrinath Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Badrinath Temple (Badarīnātha), a Divya Deśam in the Garhwal Himalayas (Uttarakhand) at 3,133 m, dedicated to Viṣṇu as Badarīnārāyaṇa. One of the four Char Dham pilgrimage sites and one of the 108 Divya Deśams glorified by the Āḻvārs (Nammāḻvār, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār). The temple houses a 1m black stone image of Viṣṇu in padmāsana. Open only six months a year (Apr-Nov); the idol is moved to Joshimath in winter. Mentioned in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham. ---

temple.title: Devaprayāga Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Raghunāthajī Temple at Devaprayāga (Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand), a Divya Deśam at the confluence of the Alaknandā and Bhāgīrathī (forming the Gaṅgā). Dedicated to Viṣṇu as Raghunāthajī (Rāma). The legendary spot where Rāma performed penance after the Rāvaṇa war. The temple was rebuilt by the Garhwal kings. Glorified by Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The annual Rāma-navamī and the Gaṅgā-avataraṇa (Gaṅgā descent) festivals are celebrated. One of the five Prayāga confluences. ---

temple.title: Dvārakā Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Dvārakādhīśa Temple (Dvārakā), a Divya Deśam on the Gujarat coast, dedicated to Viṣṇu as Dvārakādhīśa (Lord of Dvārakā). One of the four Char Dham and one of the 108 Divya Deśams. The original temple is attributed to Vajranābha (Kṛṣṇa's great-grandson); the current structure dates to 15th-16th century. The five-storey śikhara rises 78m. Glorified by Nammāḻvār and Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham. The Kṛṣṇa janmabhūmi and the nearby Bet Dwarka (Śāṇṭipura) are associated sites. ---

temple.title: Guruvāyūr Temple (Kṛṣṇa)
temple.description: The Guruvāyūr Temple (ഗുരുവായൂര്‍ / குருவாயூர்) in Thrissur district, Kerala — "Bhūloka Vaikuṇṭha" (Vaikuṇṭha on Earth). Dedicated to Kṛṣṇa as Guruvāyūrapurṇan (the Lord of Guruvāyūr), a four-armed standing Viṣṇu with conch, discus, mace, lotus. The idol is said to be worshipped by Vāyu and Bṛhaspati (hence Guru-vāyūr). Kerala architecture: copper-plated roof, golden flagstaff (dvaja-stambha), the Chuttambalam (circumambulatory). Famous for elephants (Punnathur Kotta — elephant sanctuary), the daily uṣa-pūjā (3:30 AM), and the Guruvāyūr Śrī Kṛṣṇa Suprabhātam. The annual Ekādaśī (Vṛścika Ekādaśī, Nov-Dec) and the Utsavam (festival, Feb-Mar) with the Āna-yoṭṭam (elephant race) draw millions. The temple's unique appam-prasādam (rice cake) and the Guruvāyūr Devaswom management. --- The Guruvāyūr Temple in Kerala, a major Kṛṣṇa pilgrimage site with distinctive Kerala architecture and elephant traditions; its daily rituals and festival calendar are represented here as a catalogue entry.

temple.description: The Jagannātha Temple at Purī (Odisha), a Divya Deśam and one of the four Char Dham, dedicated to Viṣṇu as Jagannātha (Lord of the Universe) with Balabhadra and Subhadrā. The iconic wooden deities are renewed every 12-19 years (Nabakalebara). The massive Ratha-yātrā festival draws millions. Glorified by all twelve Āḻvārs in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham. The temple kitchen (Mahāprasāda) serves 10,000+ daily. The Govardhana-maṭha of Śaṅkara is located here. ---

temple.title: Jyotirmaṭha Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Narasiṃha Temple at Jyotirmaṭha (Joshimath, Uttarakhand), a Divya Deśam and the winter seat of the Badrinath deity. Dedicated to Viṣṇu as Narasiṃha (the man-lion avatāra). One of the four Maṭhas established by Ādi Śaṅkara (the Uttara Maṭha). The deity is believed to be self-manifested (svayambhū). The temple is at 1,890m elevation. Glorified by Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The annual Narasiṃha-jayantī and the Badrinath opening/closing ceremonies are centered here. The nearby Kalpavṛkṣa and the cave of Ādi Śaṅkara are pilgrimage sites. ---

temple.title: Kāñcī Varadarāja Perumal Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Varadarāja Perumal Temple (Devarāja-svāmī) at Kāñcīpuram (Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Varadarāja (the King who grants boons). The 11th-century Cōḷa structure with a 100-pillar mandapa and the Athi Varadar (the original wooden deity) preserved in the temple tank. Glorified by Nammāḻvār, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār, Poygai Āḻvār, and Bhūta Āḻvār. One of the Kāñcī Divya Deśams along with Yathothkāri, Ulagalantha Perumal, and others. The Garuḍa-sevā festival is famous. ---

temple.title: Nācciyār Kōyil Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Nācciyār Kōyil (Tirunāṟaiyūr) at Tiruppanandal near Kumbakonam (Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Śrīnivāsa Perumāl with Goddess Nācciyār (Lakṣmī). The Cōḷa-period temple where Lakṣmī is enshrined as the primary deity (Nācciyār) — unique among Divya Deśams. Glorified by Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār and Nammāḻvār. The annual Garuḍa-sevā and the Tiruppāvai festival (Mārgaḻi) are celebrated. The temple architecture follows the madhyama (medium) type. ---

temple.title: Oppiliappan Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Oppiliappan Temple (Uppiliappan) near Kumbakonam (Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Oppiliappan (the Lord who accepts even saltless offerings). The legend: Lakṣmī as Bhūmidevi offered food without salt; Viṣṇu accepted it, hence "Uppu-illa-appan" (Lord without salt). No salt is used in the temple kitchen. Glorified by Nammāḻvār and Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The temple tank (Tula-puṣkariṇī) and the annual Pavitrotsavam are notable. ---

temple.title: Rāmeśvaram Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Rāmanāthasvāmī Temple at Rāmeśvaram (Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam and one of the four Char Dham, dedicated to Viṣṇu as Rāmanātha (Rāma's Lord) — here Viṣṇu and Śiva are worshipped together. One of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas (Rāmanāthaliṅga). The longest temple corridor in India (1,220m with 1,212 pillars). Glorified by Nammāḻvār, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār, and Kulasekhara Āḻvār. The sacred tīrthas (22 wells) within the complex. The Sethu (Adam's Bridge) to Śrī Lanka is nearby. ---

temple.title: Sabarimala Temple (Ayyappa)
temple.description: The Ayyappa Temple at Sabarimala (ശബരിമല / சபரிமலை), Kerala, in the Periyar Tiger Reserve (Western Ghats) at 914m elevation. A major pilgrimage site (40-50 million annually, Nov-Jan) with a distinctive 41-day vrata (maṇḍala kālam / മണ്ഡല കാലം): black/blue clothes, brahmacarya, daily bath, no shaving, no footwear, vegetarian diet. The 18 holy steps (paṭinēṭṭāmpaṭi / பதினெட்டாம்படி) represent the 18 purāṇas/18 guṇas; only those carrying the irumuḍi (sacred bundle) may ascend. The deity is a yogic Śāstā in chin-mudrā. Makaravilakku (Makara Jyoti) on Makara Saṅkrānti (Jan 14/15) is the climax. The Vāvaru (Muslim devotee) shrine at Erumeli and the Peta (Petty) shrine en route exemplify communal harmony. The river Pampa is the sacred bathing ghāṭ. Managed by the Travancore Devaswom Board. --- The Ayyappa Temple at Sabarimala, Kerala, a major pilgrimage site with a distinctive 41-day vrata and seasonal opening; its history, forest setting, and Makaravilakku are represented here as a catalogue entry.

temple.title: Śrīraṅgam Sāraṅgāpani Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Sāraṅgāpani Temple at Kumbakonam (Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Sāraṅgāpani (holding the bow Sāraṅga). The 12th-century Cōḷa temple with a 50m tall gopura and the unique chariot-shaped (ratha) sanctum. The chariot festival (Rathotsava) is famous. Glorified by Nammāḻvār, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār, Poygai Āḻvār, and Periyalvār. The temple tank (Hema-puṣkariṇī) is sacred. One of the five Pañcarātra temples (with Śrīraṅgam, Tirupati, Kāñcī, and Badrinath). ---

temple.title: Simhācalam Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Varāha Narasiṃha Temple at Simhācalam (Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Varāha Narasiṃha (the boar-man-lion form). The deity is covered in sandalwood paste year-round (revealed only on Akṣaya Tritīyā). The Kalinga-style architecture with a 96-pillar mandapa. Glorified by Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The annual Candana-yātrā (sandalwood procession) and the Narasiṃha-jayantī are major festivals. One of the few Divya Deśams with a Narasiṃha primary deity. ---

temple.title: Śrīraṅgam Ranganatha Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Śrī Raṅganātha Temple at Śrīraṅgam (Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu), the foremost Divya Deśam and the largest functioning Hindu temple complex (156 acres). Dedicated to Viṣṇu as Raṅganātha (reclining on Ādiśeṣa). Seven concentric prākāras, 21 gopuras (the Rājagopuram is 73m, Asia's tallest). The Āḻvār tradition: all twelve Āḻvārs glorified it; Nammāḻvār's Tiruvāymoḻi was first recited here. The annual Vaikuṇṭha Ekādaśī (21-day festival) draws millions. The temple houses the Āḻvār sannidhis and the Rāmānuja's sanctum. ---

temple.title: Tirukkoṣṭiyūr Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Tirukkoṣṭiyūr Temple (Sowrīrāja Perumāl) in Sivaganga district (Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam where Viṣṇu taught the Tirumantra (Oṃ Namo Nārāyaṇāya) to Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The deity is Sowrīrāja Perumāl with Śrīdevi and Bhūdevi. The temple is the birthplace of Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār's guru (Nampiḷḷai). Glorified by Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār and Nammāḻvār. The annual Tirumantra-upadeśa festival commemorates the teaching. ---

temple.title: Tirukkurunkudi Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Nambi Temple at Tirukkurunkudi (Tirunelveli district, Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Nambi (the Lord) in a standing posture with Śrīdevi and Bhūdevi. At the foot of the Western Ghats (Mahendragiri Hills). The Cōḷa-period temple with a beautiful vimāna and the Tirupparkadal (milk ocean) tank. Glorified by Nammāḻvār (who was born nearby) and Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The annual Brahmotsavam and the Nammāḻvār-avatāra-utsavam are major festivals. One of the southernmost Divya Deśams. ---

temple.title: Tirumukkūḍal Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Tirumukkūḍal Temple at Kumbakonam (Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam dedicated to the three deities in one: Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa), Brahmā, and Rudra (Śiva). The temple represents the concept of Trimūrti in one form (Tirumukkūḍal = "three-joined"). ---

temple.title: Tirunāvāya Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Navamukunda Temple at Tirunāvāya (Malappuram, Kerala), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Navamukunda (nine-faced). On the banks of the Bhāratappuzha (Nīlā) river. The annual Karkkaṭaka-vāvu (ancestor rites) draws thousands. The temple is associated with the Māmāṅkam festival (medieval trade fair). Glorified by Nammāḻvār and Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The Kerala-style architecture with a round sanctum (vṛtta-śikhara). One of the few Divya Deśams in Kerala. ---

temple.title: Tiruppāṟkaṭal Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Tiruppāṟkaṭal Temple (the Ocean of Milk) at Kāñcīpuram (Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam where Viṣṇu reclines on Ādiśeṣa in the Kṣīrasāgara (ocean of milk). The temple is associated with the Pāṟkaṭal (the milk ocean) where the Devas and Asuras churned for amṛta. Glorified by Poygai Āḻvār, Bhūta Āḻvār, and Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The annual Kṣīrābdhi-navamī festival celebrates the churning. A small but theologically important Divya Deśam representing the cosmic ocean. ---

temple.title: Tiruppullāṇi Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Ādi Jagannātha Temple at Tiruppullāṇi (near Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Ādi Jagannātha (the original Jagannātha) in a reclining posture. The legend: Rāma performed śrāddha for his father Daśaratha here; the temple marks the spot where Rāma prayed to Viṣṇu before crossing to Lanka. The sacred tīrtha (Darbha-śayana-tīrtha) is famous. Glorified by Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār and Nammāḻvār. The annual Rāma-navamī and the Ādi-amāvāsyā festivals are celebrated. ---

temple.title: Tiruvallikēṇi Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Pārthasārathi Temple at Tiruvallikēṇi (Triplicane, Chennai, Tamil Nadu), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Pārthasārathi (Kṛṣṇa as Arjuna's charioteer). The 8th-century Pallava temple, expanded by the Cōḷas and Vijayanagara. Five sancta: Pārthasārathi, Ranganātha, Rāma, Narasiṃha, and Varāha. The temple tank (Kairavinī) is famous for the float festival (Teppa-utsavam). Glorified by Poygai Āḻvār, Bhūta Āḻvār, Pēy Āḻvār, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār, and Nammāḻvār. One of the oldest Divya Deśams in an urban setting. ---

temple.description: The Anantasayana Temple at Tiruvānana-pura (Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Anantasayana (reclining on the cosmic serpent). The deity is in reclining posture on Ādiśeṣa, with the hill temple offering a panoramic view. The annual Anavasyava Ekādaśī and the annual temple car festival are celebrated. Glorified by Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The temple gives its name to the city of Thiruvananthapuram. ---

temple.title: Tṛkkākkāra Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Tṛkkākkāra Temple (Vāmana Mūrti) at Tṛkkākkāra near Kochi (Kerala), a Divya Deśam dedicated to Viṣṇu as Vāmana (the dwarf avatāra). The only Divya Deśam in Kerala proper. The legend: Vāmana placed his third step on Mahābali's head here. The annual Onam festival (ten days) celebrates Mahābali's visit, culminating in the Vāmana-jayantī. Glorified by Nammāḻvār and Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār. The temple follows the Kerala architectural style with a copper-plated roof. ---

temple.title: Tirumala Tirupati Divya Deśam
temple.description: The Veṅkaṭeśvara Temple at Tirumala (Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh), a Divya Deśam and the most visited pilgrimage site in India (30-40 million annually). Dedicated to Viṣṇu as Veṅkaṭeśvara (Lord of Veṅkaṭa Hill). The Dravidian architecture with gold-plated vimāna (Ananda Nilayam). Glorified by Nammāḻvār, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār, Kulasekhara Āḻvār, and Tiruppaṇ Āḻvār. The Tirumalā-Tirupati Devasthānams (TTD) manages the temple. The Brahmotsavam (9-day festival) and the weekly Śeṣa-vāhana-sevā are major events. The laddū-prasādam is world-famous. ---
